paras: The lynching of Jack Turner took place at Butler, the county seat of Choctaw County, Alabama, on August 19, 1882, when a crowd took Turner, a Black Republican leader, from jail and hanged him on the vote of a mass meeting. He had been jailed with several other Black men on the charge of leading a plot to massacre the county's white population, a charge resting on papers said to have been found by two white men. Republican papers and Black Republicans called the plot an invention meant to intimidate Black voters, and the governor's office asked county officers for an investigation, which they answered with a defense of the hanging.

Turner was described as chairman of the county Republican executive committee and the recognized leader of the Black population of Choctaw County. He had testified in federal court at Mobile in June 1882 against violators of the election laws, and had pressed a federal case against a planter who whipped a laborer for voting Republican.

According to a Mobile dispatch, on August 15 two white men found a bundle of papers describing a 400-member conspiracy, dating from 1878, to kill every white person in the county, and laid them before the solicitor. A citizens' meeting at Butler decided to arrest seven alleged ringleaders, among them Jack Turner, F. D. Barney, Jesse Wilson and Peter Hill. Armed white men seized them and lodged them in jail at Butler on August 17, according to a Meridian dispatch.

On Saturday morning, August 19, prisoners were taken out and questioned under torture: the Meridian dispatch said 'Secretary Fred. Bonner' was 'tied up by the toes' and a preacher named Limon was whipped until he spoke of the plot. A mass meeting of about 700 people, said to include about 150 Black men, heard the papers read and voted that Turner was 'a regular firebrand' whose immediate death the public demanded.

Turner was taken from the jail and hanged to the limb of a tree on the main street of Butler around midday, in the presence of the crowd. The Mobile Gazette reported that he was hanged from his own cart and that men afterward rode their horses over his body.

On August 30 Governor Cobb's private secretary, Robert McKee, wrote to Solicitor George W. Taylor that Turner had been 'murdered' while in the hands of officers and asked for a full investigation. Taylor, Sheriff John A. Harmon and six other county officers replied that the people had acted under 'imperious and impending necessity'; no report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

Black Republicans organized protests: the Arthur Republican Club of Mobile on August 25 called the plot 'fabulous' and asked the President and Attorney General for federal arrests. Alabama colored Republicans in Washington called for protest meetings in every county on October 15 and named a committee to investigate.

The first report, a Mobile dispatch of August 21, ran in papers across the country on August 22 under headings such as 'A Negro Plot Unearthed in Alabama' and 'Bloodthirsty Negroes,' and told the plot as fact. A Meridian version in the Pascagoula Democrat-Star called Turner 'a notoriously bad negro' and said the hanging was 'as deliberate as if done under the forms of law.'

The Washington National Republican printed the wire under the head 'The Latest Murder by a Mob' and mocked it the next day in 'A Quiet Negro Hunt.' The Sacramento Record-Union dismissed the 'cock-and-bull story,' and the New York Tribune quoted an observer who called it a device of the freedmen's enemies.

William V. Turner's letter to the National Republican protested that Black men were hanged 'upon trumped up pretexts,' and the Huntsville Gazette, writing for 'our people,' demanded a state investigation of a lynching carried out 'without judge or jury.' Within Alabama, the Montgomery Advertiser described the torture while crediting the plot, and the Democratic Eutaw Mirror wrote that the hanging was murder in law.

The plot rested on the found papers, on confessions taken under the whip, and on the county officers' word, while Republicans and the Mobile Gazette called the records forged; in October the Gazette said a Butler Democrat had named a white Democrat as their author.

reader.title: Lynching of Jack Turner
bases: A crowd at Butler took Jack Turner from jail and hanged him on the vote of a mass meeting, with no trial (A2, A17, A33).

Turner was hanged in the presence of a meeting of some 700 people who voted his death on the charge of leading a plot, while he was held in jail without trial (A2, A17); the governor's office called it the act of a mob and county officers wrote that the people 'took the law into their own hands' (A33).

The Mobile wire, a separate Meridian dispatch, the Mobile Register letter, the Mobile Gazette account and the county officers' own reply all agree that Turner was taken from jail and hanged at Butler; only the alleged plot is disputed (A2, A17, A24, A32, A33).

accounts.label: Mobile wire / Mobile Register correspondent
accounts.gist: Papers revealed a 400-man plot set for a September camp-meeting night; seven ringleaders were arrested and a meeting of about 700 voted Turner's death, after which he was hanged about 1:15 p.m. and all was quiet.

accounts.label: Meridian dispatch
accounts.gist: Armed whites seized Turner and others; prisoners were tied up by the toes and whipped for confessions, and Turner was taken from jail and hanged to a tree on the main street between 12 and 1.

accounts.label: Mobile Gazette / Moses Turner
accounts.gist: The records were 'trumped up' to remove active Black Republicans; Turner was hanged from his own cart and men rode horses over his body.

accounts.label: Black Republicans
accounts.gist: The plot was invented by the mob to excuse a political murder and frighten Black voters before the fall elections.

accounts.label: Choctaw County officers
accounts.gist: The people acted out of 'imperious and impending necessity' to save many lives.

framing.detail: Southern wire heads such as 'A Negro Plot Unearthed' and 'A Fiendish Plot ... The Leader Hung' presented the plot as fact and the hanging as orderly.
Northern and western papers ran the Mobile wire or short briefs without comment.
Republican papers (National Republican, Sacramento Record-Union, New York Tribune) called the plot a 'cock-and-bull story' and the hanging political terrorism.
The Huntsville Gazette, speaking for 'our people', printed Black Republican resolutions and asked the state for an investigation.
The Montgomery Advertiser reported the torture and believed in Turner's guilt, while the Democratic Eutaw Mirror called the hanging murder.
